title: Where History Happened
subtitle: The Places That Made and Kept Him
intro: A Manhattan brownstone, a cabin on the Little Missouri, a hill above Oyster Bay, a library in Buffalo where he took an oath he never expected. Fifteen questions on the places Roosevelt's life turned.
heroAlt: Theodore Roosevelt's birthplace at 28 East 20th Street, New York
heroCredit: Theodore Roosevelt's birthplace, 28 East 20th Street, New York. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

badge.title: Where History Happened
badge.shareText: I scored {score}/{total} on the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library's Homes and Places quiz — {tier}. Try it:

questions.explanation: A brownstone at 28 East 20th Street. It was demolished in 1916 and reconstructed as a memorial after his death; today it is the Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace National Historic Site — a rebuilt house standing where the original stood.
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt's birthplace, 28 East 20th Street, New York. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What was Roosevelt's lifelong home at Oyster Bay called?
questions.explanation: Sagamore Hill, built in 1884–85 and named for the Sagamore Mohannis, a chief who had signed away rights to the land generations before. Roosevelt lived there until he died in his sleep in an upstairs room in January 1919.
questions.credit: The Parlor, Sagamore Hill. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What were Roosevelt's two Dakota ranches called?
options: The Little Missouri and the Elkhorn
The Bar-T and the Circle Dot
The Maltese Cross and the Elkhorn
questions.explanation: The Maltese Cross, also called Chimney Butte, about seven miles south of Medora; and the Elkhorn, roughly thirty-five miles north in a bend of the river, deliberately far from anyone. The Maltese Cross was a going concern he bought into; the Elkhorn he had built from scratch, and it was the one he called his home ranch.
questions.credit: Maltese Cross Ranch house as it was when T.R. lived there. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What remains at the Elkhorn Ranch site today?
options: Nothing is known of the location
Foundation stones and the site itself
questions.explanation: Foundation stones, cottonwoods and the bend of the Little Missouri. The site sits within Theodore Roosevelt National Park and is often called the Cradle of Conservation. Getting there still requires effort, which is arguably the point.
questions.imageAlt: The Elkhorn Ranch house among cottonwoods on the Little Missouri
questions.credit: Elkhorn Ranch, Roosevelt's property on the Little Missouri. Photograph by Theodore Roosevelt. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University. Cropped from the cabinet-card mount.

questions.prompt: Who founded the town of Medora, and after whom was it named?
options: The Marquis de Mores, after his wife
The Northern Pacific Railroad, after a director
questions.explanation: The Marquis de Mores founded it on April 1, 1883, and named it for his wife, Medora von Hoffman. His chateau still overlooks the town, and the ruined chimney of his beef-packing plant still stands.
questions.imageAlt: The house of the Marquis de Mores above the Little Missouri
questions.credit: The house of the Marquis de Mores from the eastern bank of the river. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Where did Roosevelt take the presidential oath in 1901?
questions.explanation: In the library of Ansley Wilcox's house in Buffalo, hours after McKinley died, wearing borrowed formal clothes. Wilcox was a friend, and Roosevelt had been staying with him through the vigil; the oath was administered in a private parlour with a few dozen people standing about. The house is now the Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt at Buffalo during McKinley's illness
questions.credit: Vice-President Roosevelt being interviewed at Buffalo during President McKinley's illness. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt officially rename the Executive Mansion in 1901?
questions.explanation: The White House. People had used the name informally for decades; Roosevelt put it on the stationery and made it official that October.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt in his private office
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, 26th President of the United States, in his private office. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. One frame of a stereograph card; publisher's mount and caption strip removed.

questions.prompt: What came out of the 1902 White House renovation Edith Roosevelt drove?
options: The Oval Office in its current form
The North Portico and its columns
questions.explanation: The executive offices were moved out of the family's living space into a new wing on the west side — room for a presidential staff of thirty-eight, and a room of their own for the reporters, who had until then loitered in the entrance hall. Charles McKim gutted the building to do it. The Oval Office itself came later, under Taft.
questions.imageAlt: Théobald Chartran's painted portrait of Edith Kermit Roosevelt in a plumed hat, seated on a stone bench in a garden
questions.credit: Théobald Chartran's 1902 portrait of Edith Kermit Roosevelt, photographed by Frances Benjamin Johnston. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Which national park bears Roosevelt's name?
questions.explanation: Theodore Roosevelt National Park, in the Badlands of western North Dakota — the only national park named for a single person. Its three units are the South Unit at Medora, the North Unit up near Watford City, and the Elkhorn Ranch site between them. The Maltese Cross cabin stands behind the South Unit visitor centre, having been moved several times before it came home.
questions.imageAlt: The Little Missouri River in the Badlands
questions.credit: "A plains river" — the Little Missouri. Photograph by Theodore Roosevelt. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Where did Roosevelt marry his first wife, Alice Hathaway Lee?
questions.explanation: In the Unitarian church at Brookline, Massachusetts, on October 27, 1880 — his twenty-second birthday. His second marriage, to Edith, took place at St George's, Hanover Square, in London six years later.
questions.imageAlt: Alice Hathaway Lee, the first Mrs. Theodore Roosevelt
questions.credit: The first Mrs. Theodore Roosevelt (Alice Hathaway Lee). Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Where was Roosevelt when he learned McKinley was dying?
options: Already in Buffalo at the bedside
questions.explanation: On Mount Marcy, the highest peak in New York. He had gone climbing after McKinley seemed to rally, partly to reassure a country that was reading the bulletins hour by hour. A guide brought the message up the mountain and he came down through the night by buckboard, changing horses in the dark, to catch a train at North Creek — by which time McKinley was already dead and Roosevelt was president.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt at Buffalo during McKinley's illness
questions.credit: Vice-President Roosevelt being interviewed at Buffalo during President McKinley's illness. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Where did Roosevelt deliver the "Man in the Arena" speech?
questions.explanation: At the Sorbonne in Paris on April 23, 1910, in an address titled “Citizenship in a Republic,” given on his way home from Africa. The arena passage is a short stretch of a long speech. He spoke at Oxford that June and at Osawatomie that August as well, which is part of why the three get muddled — 1910 was a year of large speeches in large halls.
questions.credit: "A young head on old shoulders." Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: For seven summers Roosevelt ran the country from Oyster Bay. Where did his staff actually work?
options: Rented rooms in the village, down the hill from the house
In a railroad car parked on a siding at the station
On the ground floor of the house itself
Aboard a Navy yacht moored in the bay
questions.explanation: Roosevelt kept house and office apart. The executive staff rented space in the village below — the Oyster Bay Bank Building in the summer of 1902, and from 1903 through his last presidential summer in 1908 the new Moore Building. A secretary carried the day's cables and letters up the hill each morning, took dictation, and carried the replies back down to go out by wire to Washington. Before 1902 the house had no telephone at all: anyone who wanted Roosevelt rang the village drugstore, which sent a boy up the hill on a bicycle.
questions.imageAlt: Sagamore Hill, a large shingled house with a wide porch, seen across the lawn
questions.credit: Sagamore Hill, about 1905. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Where does the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library stand?
questions.explanation: In Medora, in the Badlands of western North Dakota — the country where he ranched, and the place he credited with making the rest of his life possible. The Library is open year-round with seasonal hours.
questions.credit: Medora in 1883 — the office and company store of the Marquis de Mores. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Besides Sagamore Hill, the Roosevelts kept one other country retreat while he was president. Where?
options: A cabin in the Virginia Piedmont, south of Charlottesville
A cottage on Campobello Island, New Brunswick
A fishing camp on the Maine coast at Islesboro
A shooting lodge in the Alleghenies of Pennsylvania
questions.explanation: Edith found it in the spring of 1905 and bought it almost on the spot: a two-storey farm-worker's cottage and fifteen acres in Albemarle County, about fourteen miles south of Charlottesville, for two hundred and eighty dollars. She called it Pine Knot, after one of her husband's favourite phrases. It had no amenities beyond a stove. Roosevelt cooked his own fried chicken on kerosene, refused a Secret Service detail, and went chiefly for the birds — on one visit he and the naturalist John Burroughs walked the fields and identified seventy-five species between them.
questions.imageAlt: Théobald Chartran's painted portrait of Edith Kermit Roosevelt in a plumed hat, seated on a stone bench in a garden
questions.credit: Théobald Chartran's 1902 portrait of Edith Kermit Roosevelt, photographed by Frances Benjamin Johnston. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.
